items.title: PROJECT INITIATION, SITE SURVEY & SCOPE BASELINE
items.phase: Lifecycle Phase: Phase 1 — Initiation & Requirements Discovery
items.goal: Phase Goal: Convert vague client wishes into an unshakeable, documented Scope Statement and capture 100% of physical site realities before pricing or ordering hardware.
items.pmbok: PMBOK Alignment: Project Scope Management (Collect Requirements, Define Scope), Project Integration Management (Project Charter).
concepts: Scope Baseline = Your Contractual Armor: If an item is not written in the Deliverables list, it does not exist. If it is not listed in Assumptions & Exclusions, the client will expect it for free.

The 360° Site Survey Protocol: Site surveys are technical risk inspections, not casual strolls. You must verify cable pathways, rack U-space, electrical breaker capacity, ceiling types (plenum, drywall, open deck), and core drill requirements.

The Exclusionary Clause Doctrine: In low-voltage and IT, exclusions make the profit. Explicitly stating "120V AC power by others," "patching and painting by others," and "conduit pathways by others" saves thousands of dollars.

sequence.concept: Concept: Scope Definition & Site Survey Verification.
sequence.example: Technical Example: Client asks for "enterprise Wi-Fi coverage across our 60,000 sq ft manufacturing warehouse and cold storage facility.
sequence.problem: Business Problem: The technician finds metal shelving racks 25 feet high stacked with liquid pallets (extreme RF attenuation) and reinforced concrete walls requiring exterior penetrations. The original bid assumed drywall and open air; signal drops dead, and client refuses payment.
sequence.workshop: Integrated Workshop: Workshop 2: Stakeholder Mapping & Site Walk for a Fire Alarm Replacement in an Occupied Healthcare Wing, and Workshop 13: Site Survey & Technical Assessment for Enterprise Wi-Fi & Industrial Warehouse Video.
sequence.deliverable: Deliverable Produced: Comprehensive Technical Site Survey Checklist & Formal Project Scope Statement.
sequence.application: Field Application: Foremen complete the digital site survey form on mobile tablets with timestamped photos before any proposal is finalized.

items.title: PLANNING — WBS, SCHEDULE, COST, MARGIN & RISK
items.goal: Phase Goal: Break the project down into work packages, map the Critical Path, secure labor margins, identify equipment lead-time traps, and build an executable project baseline.
items.pmbok: PMBOK Alignment: Project Scope Management (Create WBS), Project Schedule Management, Project Cost Management, Project Risk Management.
concepts: Work Breakdown Structure (WBS) as Trade Milestones: Decomposing a job into Rough-In (pathways, cable pull), Trim-Out (devices, terminations), Head-End/Racks (patch panels, switches, NVRs, controllers), and Commissioning (programming, testing).

Critical Path & Long-Lead Equipment Bottlenecks: Identifying dependencies. You cannot pull wire before conduit is inspected; you cannot commission cameras before the core switch is powered. Access control panels with a 14-week factory lead time dictate the cutover date.
The Fully Burdened Labor Rate & Margin Protection: Calculating real labor cost (wages + payroll taxes + insurance + vehicle + non-billable tool time) to ensure bids don't sell labor at a loss.
Risk Identification: What Can Blow Up the Job?: Rating probability and financial impact for technical unknowns (asbestos ceilings, no PoE headroom, customer network firewall blocks).

sequence.concept: Concept: Critical Path Method (CPM) and Cost Breakdown.
sequence.example: Technical Example: Deploying a 12-door access control and 32-camera IP surveillance system across a regional bank branch network.
sequence.problem: Business Problem: The PM assigns two technicians without checking lead times. The specialized motorized crash bars take 8 weeks to arrive from Germany. The branch cannot open, the GC levies $1,000/day liquidated damages, and technicians sit idle.
sequence.workshop: Integrated Workshop: Workshop 3: WBS Decomposition for a Multi-Site CCTV & Access Control Rollout, and Workshop 4: CPM Scheduling & Resource Leveling Under Severe Equipment Lead-Time Constraints.
sequence.deliverable: Deliverable Produced: WBS Dictionary, Critical Path Gantt Schedule, and Trade Cost Estimating / Margin Worksheet.
sequence.application: Field Application: Every job over 40 technician hours requires a baseline schedule showing equipment ordering deadlines and milestone dependencies.

items.title: PROCUREMENT, PRE-STAGING & MOBILIZATION
items.goal: Phase Goal: Prevent dry runs and field delays by locking down supplier orders, tracking deliveries against project milestones, and pre-staging/testing equipment in the shop before arriving on site.
items.pmbok: PMBOK Alignment: Project Procurement Management, Project Resource Management.
concepts: The "Shop First, Field Second" Pre-Staging Doctrine: Never unbox an IP camera, access control panel, or network switch on a customer's floor. Pre-address IP devices, update firmware, label MAC addresses, and verify default passwords in the controlled comfort of the company shop.

Bill of Materials (BOM) Lead-Time Tagging: Categorizing materials into Stock Items (screws, patch cords, modular jacks), Standard Distributor Items (Cat6 cable, standard cameras: 3-5 days), and Critical Long-Lead Items (enterprise core switches, custom fire graphic annunciators: 6-16 weeks).
The Mobilization Gate Review: A strict rule: No technician rolls to the site until 100% of rough-in materials, rental lifts, parking passes, and safety permits are verified in the shop staging bay.

sequence.concept: Concept: Staging Verification and Supplier Management.
sequence.example: Technical Example: An enterprise deployment of 48 VoIP phones, 4 PoE switches, and a session border controller (SBC).
sequence.problem: Business Problem: Technicians arrive on site on Monday morning. They spend 5 hours unboxing equipment, finding out two switches have DOA (Dead on Arrival) power supplies, and realize the field termination plugs are the wrong wire gauge for Cat6A shielded cable. A full day of billable labor is wasted.
sequence.workshop: Integrated Workshop: Workshop 8: Subcontractor & Procurement Management for a Structured Cabling Sub Behind Schedule, and Workshop 14: Supplier Quotation Analysis, BOM Comparison & Lead-Time Optimization.
sequence.deliverable: Deliverable Produced: Master Procurement & Delivery Tracking Log, Pre-Staging Verification Checklist.
sequence.application: Field Application: Staging bay protocol: The technician signs off the "Job Box" 24 hours prior to roll-out.

items.title: FIELD EXECUTION, SITE MANAGEMENT & COMMUNICATION
items.phase: Lifecycle Phase: Phase 4 — Execution & Field Management
items.goal: Phase Goal: Run an organized, professional jobsite, coordinate seamlessly with other trades (electrical, drywall, HVAC), communicate clearly with the client, and enforce safety and technical standards daily.
items.pmbok: PMBOK Alignment: Project Communications Management, Project Resource Management, Project Stakeholder Engagement.
concepts: The 5-Minute Morning Tailgate Meeting: The foreman aligns the crew every morning: What are we completing today? What are the safety hazards (lifts, energized panels)? What materials are missing? What coordination is needed with the GC?

The "Non-Technical Client" Translation Filter: Communicating technical progress without confusing or intimidating the client. Speaking in terms of operational capabilities rather than cable standards and VLAN tags.

Trade Coordination & Pathway Sovereignty: Protecting your low-voltage cable tray and J-hooks from being crushed by HVAC ductwork or high-voltage conduit runs. Establishing clear boundaries with the electrical sub on Day 1.

sequence.concept: Concept: Daily Site Rhythm and Active Stakeholder Communication.
sequence.example: Technical Example: Installing structured cabling and ceiling-mount access points in an active corporate office during business hours.
sequence.problem: Business Problem: Technicians drag ladders through executive hallways, drill into drywall creating acoustic ceiling dust that triggers a fire alarm smoke detector, causing an evacuation and enraged executive leadership.
sequence.workshop: Integrated Workshop: Workshop 7: Kickoff Meeting & Change-Control Clinic for a VoIP/UC Migration Suffering Scope Creep (kickoff segment), and Workshop 18: Capstone Preparation Rapid Bid-to-Kickoff Micro-Simulation.
sequence.deliverable: Deliverable Produced: Kickoff Meeting Protocol, Daily Site Supervisor Report (DSR), Site Communication Plan.
sequence.application: Field Application: Foremen complete a digital Daily Site Report every afternoon at 4:30 PM with 3 site photos, logged technician hours, and noted site impediments.

items.title: PROJECT MONITORING, CONTROL & CHANGE DEFENSE
items.phase: Lifecycle Phase: Phase 5 — Monitoring, Control & Scope Defense
items.goal: Phase Goal: Track actual labor hours against estimated milestones, protect job profitability, identify project slippage early, and convert customer extra requests into approved, billed Change Orders.
items.pmbok: PMBOK Alignment: Project Cost Management (Control Costs), Project Schedule Management (Control Schedule), Project Scope Management (Control Scope).
concepts: Can You Just..." Defense: Training field technicians to spot informal scope expansion. If the client asks to move a camera 30 feet, add a data drop, or relocate an access control reader after conduit is run, it is billable extra work.

The 4-Sentence Change Script: Technicians do not argue or say "no." They say: "We can absolutely take care of that for you. That is outside our contracted scope. Let me document the details and get you a quick price and sign-off so our crew can keep moving.

Spend-Ahead Analysis (Lightweight Earned Value): If you have spent 70% of your labor budget but have only pulled 40% of the cable, you are in severe financial trouble. Catching this variance at Day 3 instead of Day 20 saves the company's margin.

sequence.concept: Concept: Scope Control and Variance Tracking.
sequence.example: Technical Example: During an access control installation, the customer asks to add magnetic locks to two emergency exit stairwell doors and connect them to the building fire alarm.
sequence.problem: Business Problem: The lead technician installs the maglocks without paperwork. At project end, the client refuses the $3,200 invoice, stating: "I thought that was part of the security package." Furthermore, the AHJ fails the inspection because no delayed-egress permits were filed.
sequence.workshop: Integrated Workshop: Workshop 7 (change-control clinic segment) & Workshop 15 (difficult customer meeting), supported by Workshop 6 (risk response planning).
sequence.deliverable: Deliverable Produced: 1-Page Field Change Order Request (COR) Form and Labor Tracking Dashboard.
sequence.application: Field Application: Zero work proceeds on any verbal modification until a signed Change Order is authorized.

items.title: TESTING, COMMISSIONING, QUALITY ASSURANCE & AHJ SIGN-OFF
items.phase: Lifecycle Phase: Phase 6 — Quality, Commissioning & Acceptance
items.goal: Phase Goal: Execute rigorous functional testing, pass all code and AHJ inspections on the first attempt, generate flawless certification reports, and eliminate punch-list callbacks.
items.pmbok: PMBOK Alignment: Project Quality Management, Project Integration Management.
concepts: The 3-Phase Quality Gate: Quality is not inspected at the end; it is built into the workflow.

The "AHJ Inspection Is a Performance" Rule: Preparing for the Fire Marshal or Electrical Inspector. Presenting stamped plans, cut sheets, battery calculations, and pre-tested zones in a clean binder so the inspector has zero reasons to search for defects.
The 100% Pre-Test Mandate: Never demonstrate a system to a customer or inspector that your team has not tested end-to-end 60 minutes prior.

sequence.concept: Concept: Structured Commissioning Protocols and Inspection Preparedness.
sequence.example: Technical Example: Commissioning an addressable fire alarm system and integrated access control fail-safe release in a commercial healthcare building.
sequence.problem: Business Problem: The contractor schedules the Fire Marshal inspection without testing the elevator recall and air handler shutdown. During the official test, the duct smoke detector fails to shut down the HVAC unit. The AHJ fails the building, revokes the temporary certificate of occupancy, and imposes a 30-day reinspection delay.
sequence.workshop: Integrated Workshop: Workshop 9: Testing, Commissioning & Life-Safety Authority Sign-Off Simulation.
sequence.deliverable: Deliverable Produced: Master Testing & Commissioning Protocol, AHJ Inspection Dossier.
sequence.application: Field Application: Technicians submit Fluke cable test summaries and system test sheets to the PM before scheduling any customer demonstration.

## MODULE 6: TESTING, COMMISSIONING, QUALITY ASSURANCE & AHJ SIGN-OFF
- **Target Duration:** 120 Minutes
- **Lifecycle Phase:** Phase 6 — Quality, Commissioning & Acceptance

- **PMBOK Alignment:** Project Quality Management, Project Integration Management.

### 1. Essential Concepts Translated to Trade Speech
1. **The 3-Phase Quality Gate:** Quality is not inspected at the end; it is built into the workflow.
   - *Phase A (Rough-In Gate):* Pathway support, cable bend radius, bundle tension, firestop penetrations.
   - *Phase B (Trim-Out Gate):* Termination cleanliness, labeling at both ends, rack dress, ground busbar bonding.
   - *Phase C (Functional Gate):* Fluke certs, camera focus/bitrate, door latching/REX timing, battery standby test.
2. **The "AHJ Inspection Is a Performance" Rule:** Preparing for the Fire Marshal or Electrical Inspector. Presenting stamped plans, cut sheets, battery calculations, and pre-tested zones in a clean binder so the inspector has zero reasons to search for defects.
3. **The 100% Pre-Test Mandate:** Never demonstrate a system to a customer or inspector that your team has not tested end-to-end 60 minutes prior.

### 2. Pedagogical Sequence
- **Concept:** Structured Commissioning Protocols and Inspection Preparedness.
- **Technical Example:** Commissioning an addressable fire alarm system and integrated access control fail-safe release in a commercial healthcare building.
- **Business Problem:** The contractor schedules the Fire Marshal inspection without testing the elevator recall and air handler shutdown. During the official test, the duct smoke detector fails to shut down the HVAC unit. The AHJ fails the building, revokes the temporary certificate of occupancy, and imposes a 30-day reinspection delay.
- **Integrated Workshop:** *Workshop 9: Testing, Commissioning & Life-Safety Authority Sign-Off Simulation.*
- **Deliverable Produced:** Master Testing & Commissioning Protocol, AHJ Inspection Dossier.

items.title: PROJECT HANDOVER, CLOSEOUT, FINANCIAL SETTLEMENT & MAINTENANCE SLA
items.phase: Lifecycle Phase: Phase 7 — Closure & Transition to SLA
items.goal: Phase Goal: Achieve rapid formal customer sign-off, release final billing and retention within 30 days, close out all subcontractor purchase orders, capture trade lessons learned, and convert the completed installation into an annual recurring maintenance contract (ARR).
items.pmbok: PMBOK Alignment: Project Integration Management (Close Project), Project Stakeholder Management.
concepts: The "Zero-Punch-List" Strategy: The punch list is created internally by the lead tech before the customer ever sees the site. If the customer's walk-through identifies more than 3 minor cosmetic items, the team has failed its quality gate.

The Golden Handover Dossier: The client will not release final payment without their documentation: As-built CAD/PDF drawings, IP/VLAN tables, backup configuration files on USB, equipment warranty certificates, and training sign-off sheets.

The Installation-to-SLA Pivot: The day of system acceptance is the highest-trust moment in the customer relationship. Handing over the system without presenting an Annual Preventive Maintenance Agreement is leaving 40% gross-margin recurring revenue on the table.

sequence.concept: Concept: Contractual Closeout and Service Lifecycle Monetization.
sequence.example: Technical Example: Handing over a 64-camera CCTV and VMS storage server project for a regional distribution center.
sequence.problem: Business Problem: The job completes, but the PM fails to deliver as-built drawings and password documentation. The client holds $18,000 in retention for 8 months. Two years later, cameras start failing due to dust accumulation, and the client hires a competitor because no maintenance plan was ever offered.
sequence.workshop: Integrated Workshop: Workshop 12: Full Project Closure — Punch List, As-Builts, Warranty Handover & Financial Reconciliation, and Workshop 16: Maintenance Contract Conversion & SLA Transition.
sequence.deliverable: Deliverable Produced: Formal Certificate of Acceptance, Closeout Handover Package Checklist, 1-Page Maintenance SLA Proposal.
sequence.application: Field Application: PMs deliver the complete O&M package and SLA proposal alongside the final invoice within 5 business days of commissioning.

### 2. Pedagogical Sequence

- **Technical Example:** Handing over a 64-camera CCTV and VMS storage server project for a regional distribution center.
- **Business Problem:** The job completes, but the PM fails to deliver as-built drawings and password documentation. The client holds $18,000 in retention for 8 months. Two years later, cameras start failing due to dust accumulation, and the client hires a competitor because no maintenance plan was ever offered.
- **Integrated Workshop:** *Workshop 12: Full Project Closure — Punch List, As-Builts, Warranty Handover & Financial Reconciliation, and Workshop 16: Maintenance Contract Conversion & SLA Transition.*
- **Deliverable Produced:** Formal Certificate of Acceptance, Closeout Handover Package Checklist, 1-Page Maintenance SLA Proposal.
- **Field Application:** PMs deliver the complete O&M package and SLA proposal alongside the final invoice within 5 business days of commissioning.

items.title: CONTRACT RISK, COMPLIANCE, PRIVACY & CYBER-HARDENING
items.phase: Lifecycle Phase: Cross-cutting — bid stage (contract risk), execution (permits and authority approvals), handover (privacy and cyber-hardening)
items.goal: Phase Goal: Stop signing unlimited liability, deliver systems that are lawful to operate and defensible in court, and hand over networked security systems that are not the weakest link in the client's network.
items.pmbok: PMBOK Alignment: Project Procurement Management (Contract Types), Project Risk Management, Stakeholder Engagement.
concepts: The Five Contract Traps: Uncapped indemnity; consequential damages not excluded; liquidated damages with no excusable-delay clause; "pay-when-paid" flow-down from a GC; and insurance/COI requirements you cannot actually meet. Every one is negotiable before signature and a lawsuit after.

Compliance Is a Schedule Item, Not a Formality: Permits, authority (AHJ) approval windows, engineering submittals for listed systems, and licensing/certification requirements have lead times measured in weeks. If they are not on the critical path, the schedule is fiction.

A Camera System Is a Data-Processing System: Surveillance triggers data-protection obligations in most jurisdictions: signage in monitored zones, a defined lawful basis, a retention clock (30/90 days — never "until the disk is full"), access limited to need-to-know, secure storage, an audit trail for every export, a defined response path for data-subject requests, and — in many regions — registration with the data-protection authority. Placement is restricted (never in restrooms, changing rooms, or private spaces), and audio recording usually requires its own legal basis.

Footage Without a Timestamp Is Not Evidence: Time synchronization (NTP), chain of custody, and access logs decide whether recordings are admissible. Cyber-hardening is therefore part of system quality, not an optional extra.

You Are Installing the Client's Most Hackable Asset: Cameras, NVRs, and access controllers left on default credentials, exposed management ports, and outdated firmware are the entry point ransomware uses to encrypt a business. Delivering them in that state is a defect, not a feature.

sequence.concept: Concept: Contract risk allocation, privacy compliance, and cyber-hardening as acceptance criteria.
sequence.example: Technical Example: Handing over a 60-camera city-center CCTV and access-control system for a retail client.
sequence.problem: Business Problem: The contract carried an uncapped indemnity and made the contractor "responsible for the lawful operation of the recording system"; cameras still ran default passwords; the NVR was reachable on a public management port; recordings had no set retention; and no signage informed the public. The client's counsel demands a data-protection statement, a subject-access request is filed, and ransomware enters the client's network through the NVR six months later.

sequence.deliverable: Deliverable Produced: Contract Red-Flag Register with redlines, Privacy & Data-Protection Compliance Sheet for Security Installations, Cyber-Hardening Certificate of Delivery.
sequence.application: Field Application: Every proposal carries the limitation-of-liability and exclusion clause set; every security installation is delivered with a signed privacy sheet and hardening certificate; no system ships on default credentials.

## MODULE 9 (CROSS-CUTTING): CONTRACT RISK, COMPLIANCE, PRIVACY & CYBER-HARDENING
- **Target Duration:** 120 Minutes
- **Lifecycle Phase:** Cross-cutting — bid stage (contract risk), execution (permits and authority approvals), handover (privacy and cyber-hardening)
- **Phase Goal:** Stop signing unlimited liability, deliver systems that are lawful to operate and defensible in court, and hand over networked security systems that are not the weakest link in the client's network.
- **PMBOK Alignment:** Project Procurement Management (Contract Types), Project Risk Management, Stakeholder Engagement.

### 1. Essential Concepts Translated to Trade Speech
1. **The Five Contract Traps:** Uncapped indemnity; consequential damages not excluded; liquidated damages with no excusable-delay clause; "pay-when-paid" flow-down from a GC; and insurance/COI requirements you cannot actually meet. Every one is negotiable before signature and a lawsuit after.
2. **Compliance Is a Schedule Item, Not a Formality:** Permits, authority (AHJ) approval windows, engineering submittals for listed systems, and licensing/certification requirements have lead times measured in weeks. If they are not on the critical path, the schedule is fiction.
3. **A Camera System Is a Data-Processing System:** Surveillance triggers data-protection obligations in most jurisdictions: signage in monitored zones, a defined lawful basis, a retention clock (30/90 days — never "until the disk is full"), access limited to need-to-know, secure storage, an audit trail for every export, a defined response path for data-subject requests, and — in many regions — registration with the data-protection authority. Placement is restricted (never in restrooms, changing rooms, or private spaces), and audio recording usually requires its own legal basis.
4. **Footage Without a Timestamp Is Not Evidence:** Time synchronization (NTP), chain of custody, and access logs decide whether recordings are admissible. Cyber-hardening is therefore part of system quality, not an optional extra.
5. **You Are Installing the Client's Most Hackable Asset:** Cameras, NVRs, and access controllers left on default credentials, exposed management ports, and outdated firmware are the entry point ransomware uses to encrypt a business. Delivering them in that state is a defect, not a feature.

### 2. Pedagogical Sequence
- **Concept:** Contract risk allocation, privacy compliance, and cyber-hardening as acceptance criteria.
- **Technical Example:** Handing over a 60-camera city-center CCTV and access-control system for a retail client.
- **Business Problem:** The contract carried an uncapped indemnity and made the contractor "responsible for the lawful operation of the recording system"; cameras still ran default passwords; the NVR was reachable on a public management port; recordings had no set retention; and no signage informed the public. The client's counsel demands a data-protection statement, a subject-access request is filed, and ransomware enters the client's network through the NVR six months later.
- **Integrated Workshop:** *Workshop 20: Contract Red Flags, Privacy Compliance & the Cyber-Hardening Sign-Off.*
- **Deliverable Produced:** Contract Red-Flag Register with redlines, Privacy & Data-Protection Compliance Sheet for Security Installations, Cyber-Hardening Certificate of Delivery.
- **Field Application:** Every proposal carries the limitation-of-liability and exclusion clause set; every security installation is delivered with a signed privacy sheet and hardening certificate; no system ships on default credentials.

# PART 6: WORKSHOP PORTFOLIO (WORKSHOPS 1 TO 6)

---

## WORKSHOP 1: BID/NO-BID & SCOPE DISCOVERY ON A VAGUE SECURITY-INTEGRATION RFP
- **Lifecycle Phase:** Phase 0 — Pre-Sales / Opportunity Qualification
- **Business Line:** Physical Security System Integration (CCTV + Access Control + Intrusion)
- **Realistic Scenario:** A regional property management group issues a 4-page RFP for "Turnkey Security Modernization" across a 5-building commercial office park. The RFP states: *"Provide complete CCTV coverage of all parking lots and building perimeters, card access on all perimeter doors, intrusion detection, and connection to a central monitoring station. Bid must be fixed-price lump-sum. Proposal due in 5 business days. Project must be complete in 6 weeks. 10% retention withheld for 12 months."* No drawings, no drop counts, no camera specs, and no cable pathway data are provided.
- **Learning Objectives (Observable):** 
  1. Evaluate an ambiguous RFP using a quantitative 10-criteria Bid/No-Bid Scorecard.
  2. Draft a targeted Pre-Bid Clarification Request that flushes out technical and financial traps without alienating the client.
  3. Formulate an exclusionary scope boundary statement defending the contractor against unlimited liability.
- **Prerequisite Module:** Module 0 (Pre-Sales & Opportunity Qualification).
- **Duration & Pacing:** 90 Minutes (15m Scenario Briefing & RFP Review, 40m Team Analysis & Tool Execution, 25m Cross-Team Defense & Debrief, 10m Monday-Morning Habit Transfer).
- **Group Size & Roles:** 3 to 4 participants per team:
  - *Role A: Company Owner / Sales Director* (wants the revenue, tempted to bid blind).
  - *Role B: Estimator / Senior PM* (calculates risk, identifies missing engineering data).
  - *Role C: Lead Field Technician* (evaluates physical reality: mounting heights, trenching, power).
  - *Role D: Client Representative / GC* (defends the vague RFP, presses for a cheap number).
- **Inputs & Artifacts Provided:**
  - Copy of the 4-page ambiguous RFP and sample standard GC subcontractor agreement with indemnity clauses.
  - Historical win/loss data showing margin erosion on similar "turnkey" RFPs.
- **The Task:**
  1. Score the RFP using the Bid/No-Bid Decision Scorecard.
  2. If score is below 70, formulate the exact Go/No-Go recommendation and conditions.
  3. Draft 5 mandatory Technical Clarification Questions for the client.
  4. Write a 1-paragraph Scope Assumption Statement to accompany any preliminary budgetary estimate.
- **Expected Deliverables Produced:** Completed Bid/No-Bid Scorecard, Technical Clarification Letter, and Preliminary Scope Boundary Log.
- **Facilitator Guide & Guiding Prompts:**
  - *Prompt:* "Notice the clause 'turnkey security modernization.' If the parking lot requires directional boring and conduit trenching 400 feet under asphalt, who pays for it under this wording?"
  - *Teaching Moment:* Help learners realize that submitting a lump-sum price on a vague RFP is not selling; it is gambling with company equity.
- **3 Most Common Field Mistakes & Debrief:**
  1. *Mistake:* Assuming the client will be "reasonable" later when unforeseen costs emerge. *Debrief:* Show that in fixed-price contracting, ambiguity legally favors the buyer unless explicitly excluded.
  2. *Mistake:* Spending 20 hours designing a system without knowing if the client has a realistic budget. *Debrief:* Establish the rule of the "Qualifying Phone Call" to establish budget ranges before detailed engineering.
  3. *Mistake:* Failing to identify civil work (trenching, conduit, core drilling, 120V power). *Debrief:* Teach the standard low-voltage exclusion clause: *"All conduit, pathway, coring, and 120VAC power provided by others."*
- **Assessment Rubric (1 to 4 Scale):**
  - *1 (Deficient):* Recommends bidding blind lump-sum; misses trenching and pathway risks.
  - *2 (Developing):* Identifies missing specs but fails to attach contractual assumptions to the bid.
  - *3 (Proficient):* Scores RFP objectively; writes clear pre-bid questions and standard trade exclusions.
  - *4 (Exemplary):* Successfully negotiates a paid engineering/site-survey phase with the client before bidding.
- **So What Monday Morning Transfer:** Put the 1-Page Bid/No-Bid Scorecard on the estimator's desk. Any RFP scoring below 65 is either rejected or converted into a paid discovery walk.
- **Variations (5-Person vs. 30-Person SME):**
  - *5-Person Shop:* Owner runs the scorecard solo in 10 minutes to protect limited technician time.
  - *30-Person Firm:* Estimator and Lead PM review the scorecard jointly before proposal kickoff.

---

## WORKSHOP 2: STAKEHOLDER MAPPING & SITE WALK FOR A FIRE ALARM REPLACEMENT IN AN OCCUPIED HEALTHCARE WING
- **Lifecycle Phase:** Phase 1 — Project Initiation & Site Survey
- **Business Line:** Fire Alarm & Life-Safety Systems
- **Realistic Scenario:** A 40-bed specialized sub-acute healthcare facility requires the replacement of an obsolete legacy conventional fire alarm panel with a new addressable voice-evacuation system (Notifier NFS2-3030 with voice). The facility is 100% occupied with high-dependency patients, immunocompromised wards, and locked memory-care units. Ceiling spaces are known to contain asbestos-containing insulation in older wings. Work must not trigger false alarms or disrupt patient care.
- **Learning Objectives (Observable):**
  1. Construct a comprehensive Stakeholder Register and Communication Protocol for a high-consequence healthcare environment.
  2. Conduct a simulated multi-dimensional Site Walk identifying infection control (ICRA), asbestos, and ceiling access barriers.
  3. Formulate an Infection Control & Life-Safety Phased Cutover Plan maintaining active detection 24/7.
- **Prerequisite Module:** Module 1 (Initiation & Site Survey).
- **Duration & Pacing:** 120 Minutes (20m Scenario Briefing & Healthcare Regulations, 50m Site Survey Simulation & Redlining, 35m Stakeholder Strategy Presentation, 15m Debrief).
- **Group Size & Roles:** 4 to 5 participants per team:
  - *Role A: Healthcare Facility Director* (hyper-focused on patient safety, zero false alarms, noise control).
  - *Role B: Infection Control Officer (ICRA)* (demands containment tents, HEPA vacuums, negative air pressure).
  - *Role C: Contractor Lead Fire Alarm PM* (responsible for schedule, budget, and system functionality).
  - *Role D: Field Lead Technician / Electrician* (responsible for physical wire pulls, ladder placement, device replacement).
  - *Role E: Local Fire Marshal / AHJ* (demands uninterrupted life-safety coverage during construction).
- **Inputs & Artifacts Provided:**
  - Architectural floor plan of the healthcare wing showing patient rooms, nurses' stations, and fire barriers.
  - Existing legacy fire alarm single-line drawing (incomplete).
  - Hospital Infection Control Risk Assessment (ICRA) Class IV protocol sheet.
- **The Task:**
  1. Map all internal and external stakeholders with their authority level, primary fears, and communication needs.
  2. Complete the Healthcare Site Walk Checklist identifying 8 hidden operational constraints.
  3. Create an Interim Life Safety Measures (ILSM) cutover schedule guaranteeing continuous fire alarm protection.
- **Expected Deliverables Produced:** Healthcare Stakeholder Matrix, Completed Site Walk Hazard Log, and ILSM Operational Phasing Plan.
- **Facilitator Guide & Guiding Prompts:**
  - *Prompt:* "If your technician drills into a ceiling tile in Ward B without an ICRA containment tent, what happens? Who can shut down your job site in 30 seconds?"
  - *Teaching Moment:* In life-safety and healthcare, technical installation is only 30% of the job; stakeholder and environmental compliance is 70%.
- **3 Most Common Field Mistakes & Debrief:**
  1. *Mistake:* Treating a hospital like a standard commercial office; drilling ceilings without containment. *Debrief:* Explain ICRA Class IV fines, shut-downs, and health risks.
  2. *Mistake:* Failing to coordinate with the local Fire Department before taking a legacy zone offline. *Debrief:* Demonstrate the mandatory Fire Watch procedure and AHJ notification protocols.
  3. *Mistake:* Forgetting patient rest hours and acoustic restrictions. *Debrief:* Show how labor estimates must account for off-hours, noisy-work windows (6:00 AM - 8:00 AM only).
- **Assessment Rubric (1 to 4 Scale):**
  - *1 (Deficient):* Ignores ICRA requirements; plans daytime strobe testing in active patient rooms.
  - *2 (Developing):* Recognizes asbestos and ICRA but fails to account for 24/7 fire watch labor costs.
  - *3 (Proficient):* Comprehensive stakeholder map; includes mobile dust containment and phased zone cutovers.
  - *4 (Exemplary):* Delivers a turn-key ILSM manual that the hospital safety committee approves without edits.
- **So What Monday Morning Transfer:** Before stepping foot on any occupied commercial, industrial, or healthcare site, complete the Pre-Walk Stakeholder Checklist and identify the site authority who controls work permits.
- **Variations (5-Person vs. 30-Person SME):**
  - *5-Person Shop:* Focus heavily on the practical daily cost of off-hours labor and containment equipment rental.
  - *30-Person Firm:* Establish formal role separation between the Safety Coordinator and Project Manager.

---

## WORKSHOP 3: WBS DECOMPOSITION FOR A MULTI-SITE CCTV & ACCESS CONTROL ROLLOUT ACROSS 12 RETAIL BRANCHES
- **Lifecycle Phase:** Phase 2 — Planning
- **Business Line:** Video Surveillance & Access Control
- **Realistic Scenario:** A regional credit union awards your company a contract to deploy an integrated IP video and access control solution across 12 branch locations spread over a 150-mile radius. Each branch requires: 8 IP cameras (Hanwha 4K), 1 8-channel NVR with cloud sync, 3 card access doors (Software House iSTAR Edge), intercom integration at the drive-through, and local panic button tie-ins. All branches must remain fully operational during business hours. Work must be finished in 60 calendar days.
- **Learning Objectives (Observable):**
  1. Decompose a multi-site technical integration project into a 4-level Work Breakdown Structure (WBS) with 100% rule compliance.
  2. Define measurable Work Packages with distinct completion criteria, labor budgets, and responsible roles.
  3. Standardize branch rollout packages to create a repeatable "cookie-cutter" operational template.
- **Prerequisite Module:** Module 2 (WBS, Schedule & Cost Planning).
- **Duration & Pacing:** 105 Minutes (15m WBS Theory & Multi-Site Pitfalls, 45m Team WBS Decomposition, 30m Cross-Team Review & Gap Analysis, 15m Debrief).
- **Group Size & Roles:** 3 to 4 participants per team:
  - *Role A: Senior Project Manager* (governs multi-site schedule, standardization, and branch reporting).
  - *Role B: Field Lead Foreman* (manages physical travel, rough-in, device mounting, and branch technicians).
  - *Role C: Systems Integration Programmer* (handles NVR pre-staging, IP addressing, VMS cloud enrollment, reader programming).
- **Inputs & Artifacts Provided:**
  - Branch archetype floor plan (standard retail banking layout: teller line, vault, ATM lobby, manager office, drive-through).
  - Scope overview document detailing hardware quantities and milestone deadlines.
- **The Task:**
  1. Build a graphical or indented 4-level WBS covering all phases (Central Engineering/Staging -> Branch Deployment -> Branch Commissioning -> Program Closeout).
  2. Create a WBS Dictionary entry for two critical work packages: *WP 2.3: Branch Staged Pre-Configuration* and *WP 3.4: Branch Physical Cutover & Acceptance*.
  3. Define the exact "Done" criteria for a branch to prevent technicians from leaving unfinished punch items behind.
- **Expected Deliverables Produced:** Complete Multi-Site Rollout WBS Tree, WBS Dictionary Cards for key work packages.
- **Facilitator Guide & Guiding Prompts:**
  - *Prompt:* "If your team travels 2 hours to Branch 7 and realizes the network switches haven't been configured by the bank's IT department, where did your WBS fail?"
  - *Teaching Moment:* The 100% Rule—if an activity (such as travel time, van restocking, or customer network coordination) is not in the WBS, it is not in the budget.
- **3 Most Common Field Mistakes & Debrief:**
  1. *Mistake:* Structuring the WBS by physical trade tasks only, ignoring central procurement, staging, and administrative closeout. *Debrief:* Show that staging in the shop saves 60% of field travel time.
  2. *Mistake:* Vague work package definitions (e.g., "Install Cameras" instead of "Mount, Terminate, Aim, Focus, and Capture Acceptance Snapshot"). *Debrief:* Vague definitions lead to infinite punch lists.
  3. *Mistake:* Neglecting multi-site mobilization logistics (drive time, per diem, vehicle maintenance). *Debrief:* Factor travel and logistics directly into the WBS as distinct work packages.
- **Assessment Rubric (1 to 4 Scale):**
  - *1 (Deficient):* Merely lists hardware components without chronological or logical work packages.
  - *2 (Developing):* Captures physical site work but misses pre-staging, travel logistics, and client IT coordination.
  - *3 (Proficient):* Well-structured 4-level WBS with clear work packages, dictionary definitions, and measurable completion gates.
  - *4 (Exemplary):* Produces a highly optimized, modular "cookie-cutter" WBS where any technician can execute an identical branch deployment without supervision.
- **So What Monday Morning Transfer:** Never start a multi-location job without a standardized WBS template that includes Shop Staging, Field Deployment, and Client Sign-Off gates.
- **Variations (5-Person vs. 30-Person SME):**
  - *5-Person Shop:* Consolidate WBS to 3 levels; combine staging and procurement into a single lead technician package.
  - *30-Person Firm:* Assign dedicated package owners (Central Staging Engineer vs. Mobile Field Foreman).

---

## WORKSHOP 4: CPM SCHEDULING & RESOURCE LEVELING WITH A 2-TECH CREW & LONG EQUIPMENT LEAD TIMES
- **Lifecycle Phase:** Phase 2 — Planning
- **Business Line:** Computer Networks & Structured Cabling
- **Realistic Scenario:** A distribution logistics company is expanding into a new 80,000 sq ft warehouse. The scope includes: 140 Cat6A network drops, 12 industrial wireless access points (Aruba AP-555), 2 IDF wall-mount server cabinets, and a fiber optic 10G backbone link to the main office MDF (500-foot armored multi-mode fiber pull with fusion splicing). 
  - *Resources Available:* Only 2 full-time technicians (Lead Tech Dave, Junior Tech Sam).
  - *Constraints:* The industrial PoE switches and specialized fiber patch panels have a strict 10-week factory lead time. The warehouse racking installation starts in Week 4. The concrete floor polishing starts in Week 6 (no lifts allowed on floor for 10 days). Customer occupancy date is fixed at Week 12.
- **Learning Objectives (Observable):**
  1. Construct a Critical Path Method (CPM) network diagram calculating Early Start, Early Finish, Late Start, Late Finish, and Float.
  2. Identify the true Critical Path driving the project delivery date under long procurement lead times.
  3. Perform Resource Leveling for a 2-person crew to eliminate over-allocation while respecting site access blackouts.
- **Prerequisite Module:** Module 2 (WBS, Schedule & Cost Planning).
- **Duration & Pacing:** 120 Minutes (20m Critical Path & Lead Time Mechanics, 50m Scheduling & Leveling Exercise, 35m Schedule Optimization Defense, 15m Debrief).
- **Group Size & Roles:** 3 to 4 participants per team:
  - *Role A: Project Scheduler / Operations Manager* (balances company-wide crew allocations).
  - *Role B: Lead Field Technician* (understands daily wire-pull productivity and scissor-lift constraints).
  - *Role C: General Contractor Representative* (defends the floor polishing and racking dates; refuses schedule slips).
- **Inputs & Artifacts Provided:**
  - Activity list with estimated durations (in tech-hours) and strict physical dependencies.
  - Calendar constraint sheet (concrete floor curing window, scissor lift rental dates, equipment ship dates).
- **The Task:**
  1. Build a sequenced CPM schedule identifying Total Float for all non-critical paths.
  2. Map out the 2-technician daily allocation across the 12-week timeline.
  3. Resolve the resource clash: Day 18 through Day 24 requires 3 technicians to beat the floor polisher deadline. Propose a viable contractor solution (overtime, phased pull, or pre-pulling fiber pathways).
- **Expected Deliverables Produced:** CPM Network Logic Chart, Resource-Leveled Gantt Schedule, and Lead-Time Risk Mitigation Plan.
- **Facilitator Guide & Guiding Prompts:**
  - *Prompt:* "Look at Week 1. Dave and Sam are scheduled to pull cable, but the scissor lifts haven't arrived and the unistrut isn't installed. If you start pulling wire on the floor, what happens to productivity?"
  - *Teaching Moment:* Lead times are not passive waiting periods; they are active critical path items that require milestone tracking just like physical installation.
- **3 Most Common Field Mistakes & Debrief:**
  1. *Mistake:* Scheduling installation assuming equipment is magically on site on Day 1. *Debrief:* Show how ordering equipment without tracking PO confirmation dates triggers crew idle time.
  2. *Mistake:* Over-allocating the lead tech to 60 hours in a week without factoring fatigue, rework, or vehicle travel. *Debrief:* Demonstrate sustainable 35-billable-hour scheduling models for small crews.
  3. *Mistake:* Ignoring other trades' hard site constraints (e.g., polished concrete curing). *Debrief:* Emphasize coordinating high-reach work before floor treatments or racking obstructs aerial access.
- **Assessment Rubric (1 to 4 Scale):**
  - *1 (Deficient):* Ignores the 10-week equipment lead time; creates an unexecutable schedule with massive resource clashes.
  - *2 (Developing):* Identifies lead times but fails to level technician hours; overlaps work during the concrete cure window.
  - *3 (Proficient):* Accurate CPM diagram; correctly identifies critical path; levels 2-tech crew around site blackouts.
  - *4 (Exemplary):* Optimizes the schedule by pre-pulling home-runs during empty warehouse windows, saving 15% in lift rental costs.
- **So What Monday Morning Transfer:** Whenever a quote contains equipment with a lead time exceeding 3 weeks, place an "Equipment PO Placed & Confirmed" milestone at the top of the job schedule.
- **Variations (5-Person vs. 30-Person SME):**
  - *5-Person Shop:* Focus heavily on the cash impact of rental lifts sitting idle while waiting for cable.
  - *30-Person Firm:* Cross-level technicians between two different commercial projects to absorb float.
